---
title: "Predicting Spatial Classes with Random Forest"
date: 2026-09-11
categories: [tool, geoml, bilingual]
description: "An interactive lab with Python, R and MapLibre: turn labeled points into a full classification surface with a Random Forest, see why a random train/test split flatters a map and what spatial block cross-validation reports instead, and a real gotcha where R silently swaps classification for regression."
---

A few labeled points on their own only answer questions about
themselves: "what class is point #7?" is a question you can already
answer by looking at the file. The useful question is the one you
*can't* already answer: "what's the likely class everywhere else,
including where I have no data at all?" A Random Forest trained on
labeled points, then applied to a regular grid across the whole area,
turns a sparse set of samples into a full classification surface, the
same shift in usefulness a sparse rain-gauge network gets from
interpolating a rainfall map between the gauges.

Whether that surface is worth trusting is a separate question, and one
this article measures rather than assumes, two ways: holding out
points at random, the textbook default, and holding out whole blocks
of the map. On spatial data the two give very different answers, and
section 4 shows why the second is the one to believe.

A `.geojson`, or a shapefile (either as a single `.zip`, or as
`.shp`/`.dbf`/`.shx` selected together): see the upload section
below.

Just want to classify a file with adjustable settings, any class
column, and a download button, without the rest of the reading? Use
the [standalone tool](/tools/spatial-classifier.html) — same engine,
less prose.

## 1. Why the coordinate system matters here

A Random Forest trained directly on longitude/latitude would treat 1
degree of separation as the same "distance" everywhere on Earth, which
it isn't. Both languages below pick a working UTM zone from the data's
own bounding-box center and reproject into it first, same reasoning,
same formula, as this site's [Viewshed](raster-viewshed.qmd) and
[Spatial Clustering](spatial-clustering.qmd) tools: a reasonable
default for one local dataset, not a universally correct choice for
points spanning multiple UTM zones or very large areas.

## 2. Upload your points

::: {#lab-upload}
:::

No file uploaded, or your file has no column literally named
`class`? Both cells below fall back to the same built-in survey: 30
sites, 5 points recorded close together at each, across three zones
(`south`, `centre`, `north`) whose boundaries undulate rather than
running straight. One site in five sits on a local patch of a
different class, the kind of small inclusion a real survey keeps
running into: a wet hollow in a dry field, a stand of a different
species. Both tabs build it from the same arithmetic rule instead of a
list of coordinates, so the points are identical and the two languages
are comparable.

Both details are there on purpose. Surveys really are collected in
sites like this, a handful of readings wherever someone stopped. And
the patches are what keep the scores honest: with tidy zones and
nothing unexpected inside them, any classifier would score close to
100%, which teaches nothing except misplaced confidence. Number of
trees and grid resolution are fixed here (100 trees, a 10-cell grid)
to keep the focus off tuning; the
[standalone tool](/tools/spatial-classifier.html) exposes both as
adjustable controls and lets you pick any column as the class.

## Python

```{.webgeods-python #spatial-classification-py}
#| package: geopandas, scikit-learn
import geopandas as gpd
import numpy as np
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedKFold
from sklearn.neighbors import NearestNeighbors
from shapely.geometry import Polygon

# The example survey, used only when nothing was uploaded (or the
# upload has no `class` column). Written as a rule rather than a list
# of coordinates, so the structure is visible instead of buried in 150
# pairs of numbers: 30 survey sites, 5 points recorded close together
# at each, three bands whose boundaries undulate across the area, and
# one site in five sitting on a local patch of a different class.
# Plain arithmetic only (no random numbers, no trigonometry), so the R
# tab further down builds exactly the same points.
FALLBACK_NEXT_CLASS = {"south": "centre", "centre": "north", "north": "south"}
SITE_OFFSETS = [(0, 0), (1, 0.4), (-0.6, 0.9), (-0.8, -0.7), (0.5, -1)]

def fallback_points():
    points = []
    for s in range(30):
        # Site centers on a 6 x 5 lattice, nudged off it by a fixed
        # arithmetic jitter so they don't line up in rows.
        col, row = s % 6, s // 6
        cx = (col + 0.5) / 6 + ((s * 37) % 11 - 5) / 110
        cy = (row + 0.5) / 5 + ((s * 53) % 13 - 6) / 130
        for dx, dy in SITE_OFFSETS:
            x, y = cx + dx * 0.02, cy + dy * 0.02
            # Triangular wave along x: the two band boundaries rise and
            # fall across the area instead of running straight, so no
            # single horizontal cut separates the classes.
            u, v = x * 15, y * 10
            tri = abs((2 * u) % 8 - 4) - 2
            cls = "south" if v < 3 + tri else ("centre" if v < 6 + tri else "north")
            # A local patch: every point at this site belongs to the
            # next class along. Unlike noise on single points, all five
            # site-mates share it, which is what section 4 is about.
            if s % 5 == 2:
                cls = FALLBACK_NEXT_CLASS[cls]
            points.append(((12.4450 + x * 0.0150, 41.8850 + y * 0.0120), cls))
    return points

gdf = None
for path in ["/uploaded.geojson", "/uploaded.shp", "/vsizip//uploaded.zip"]:
    try:
        gdf = gpd.read_file(path)
        break
    except Exception:
        pass

crs_warning = None
if gdf is not None and gdf.crs is None:
    gdf = gdf.set_crs("EPSG:4326")
    crs_warning = "No CRS found in the uploaded file — assuming WGS84 (EPSG:4326)."
elif gdf is not None and str(gdf.crs) != "EPSG:4326":
    gdf = gdf.to_crs("EPSG:4326")

if gdf is None or "class" not in gdf.columns:
    fallback = fallback_points()
    gdf = gpd.GeoDataFrame(
        {"class": [cls for _, cls in fallback]},
        geometry=gpd.points_from_xy(
            [pt[0] for pt, _ in fallback],
            [pt[1] for pt, _ in fallback]
        ),
        crs="EPSG:4326"
    )
    crs_warning = None

labeled = gdf[gdf["class"].notna()].copy()
labeled["class"] = labeled["class"].astype(str)

# UTM auto-pick from the bounding-box center -- see section 1 above.
minx, miny, maxx, maxy = gdf.total_bounds
center_lon = float((minx + maxx) / 2)
center_lat = float((miny + maxy) / 2)
utm_zone = int((center_lon + 180) // 6) + 1
calc_epsg = 32600 + utm_zone if center_lat >= 0 else 32700 + utm_zone

labeled_proj = labeled.to_crs(epsg=calc_epsg)
proj_x = labeled_proj.geometry.centroid.x.to_numpy()
proj_y = labeled_proj.geometry.centroid.y.to_numpy()

# A single UTM zone distorts badly, to the point of returning inf,
# for points far enough from it. Dropped here rather than failing:
# nothing in this article compares points by position across
# languages, so partial exclusion doesn't desync anything.
finite_mask = np.isfinite(proj_x) & np.isfinite(proj_y)
labeled_proj = labeled_proj[finite_mask]
X = np.column_stack([proj_x[finite_mask], proj_y[finite_mask]])
y = labeled_proj["class"].values

if len(y) == 0:
    raise ValueError(
        f"None of the labeled points could be projected into a single UTM "
        f"zone (EPSG:{calc_epsg}) -- this dataset spans too wide an area "
        "for this article's single-zone approach. Try a smaller, more "
        "local file."
    )

class_labels = sorted(set(y.tolist()))

# Two ways of splitting the points into 5 folds, for 5-fold
# cross-validation: each fold is held out in turn, a forest is trained
# on the other four, and every point ends up predicted exactly once by
# a model that never saw it.
#
# Random folds: points assigned at random, stratify keeping each
# class's share the same in every fold.
#
# Block folds: a 4 x 4 grid over the area, each block assigned to a
# fold by (bx + 2 * by) % 5, a diagonal pattern that spreads every fold
# across the whole map. Whole blocks go out together, so a held-out
# point's close neighbours are held out with it. No random numbers
# here, so the R tab gets exactly these same folds.
BLOCKS_PER_SIDE = 4
bmin = X.min(axis=0)
block_size = max(float((X.max(axis=0) - bmin).max()), 1e-6) / BLOCKS_PER_SIDE
block_xy = np.minimum(((X - bmin) // block_size).astype(int), BLOCKS_PER_SIDE - 1)
block_folds = (block_xy[:, 0] + 2 * block_xy[:, 1]) % 5

class_counts = {c: int((y == c).sum()) for c in class_labels}
# Too little to cross-validate (an uploaded file can have a class with
# one or two members): no accuracy is then reported as exactly that,
# rather than as a score of 0.
can_validate = len(class_labels) >= 2 and min(class_counts.values()) >= 5 and len(y) >= 10

def cross_validated(folds):
    predicted = np.empty(len(y), dtype=object)
    for f in np.unique(folds):
        train, test = folds != f, folds == f
        fold_model = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=100, random_state=0)
        fold_model.fit(X[train], y[train])
        predicted[test] = fold_model.predict(X[test])
    accuracy = round(float((predicted == y).mean()), 3)
    # Per class as well: one overall number can hide a model that is
    # perfect on the largest class and useless on another.
    by_class = {
        c: round(float((predicted[y == c] == c).mean()), 3) for c in class_labels
    }
    return accuracy, by_class

accuracy_random = accuracy_blocks = None
class_accuracy_random = class_accuracy_blocks = {}
if can_validate:
    random_folds = np.empty(len(y), dtype=int)
    splitter = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)
    for f, (_, test) in enumerate(splitter.split(X, y)):
        random_folds[test] = f
    accuracy_random, class_accuracy_random = cross_validated(random_folds)
    accuracy_blocks, class_accuracy_blocks = cross_validated(block_folds)

# How far each scheme's test points sit from the nearest point their
# forest trained on (median, in metres). Section 4 compares these with
# the same distance for the map's own grid cells, computed further down.
def nearest_distances(train_pts, query_pts):
    return NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=1).fit(train_pts).kneighbors(query_pts)[0][:, 0]

def median_test_distance(folds):
    return float(np.median(np.concatenate([
        nearest_distances(X[folds != f], X[folds == f]) for f in np.unique(folds)
    ])))

distance_random = round(median_test_distance(random_folds)) if can_validate else None
distance_blocks = round(median_test_distance(block_folds)) if can_validate else None

# X is (x, y) coordinates only: position is the ONLY predictor here.
# This demonstrates how a Random Forest turns labeled points into a
# surface, not a general land-cover classifier. Real covariates
# (spectral bands, elevation, soil type) would change what the model
# is actually learning. The map itself uses a forest trained on every
# point: the folds above were only for scoring it.
model = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=100, random_state=0)
model.fit(X, y)

# Regular 10x10-ish square-cell grid over the full extent, at a fixed
# resolution: keeps the focus on how the two languages disagree,
# rather than on tuning parameters.
gdf_proj = gdf.to_crs(epsg=calc_epsg)
full_x = gdf_proj.geometry.centroid.x.to_numpy()
full_y = gdf_proj.geometry.centroid.y.to_numpy()
full_finite_mask = np.isfinite(full_x) & np.isfinite(full_y)
gminx, gmaxx = float(full_x[full_finite_mask].min()), float(full_x[full_finite_mask].max())
gminy, gmaxy = float(full_y[full_finite_mask].min()), float(full_y[full_finite_mask].max())
width, height = gmaxx - gminx, gmaxy - gminy
cell_size = max(width, height, 1e-6) / 10
n_cols = max(1, int(np.ceil(width / cell_size)))
n_rows = max(1, int(np.ceil(height / cell_size)))

centers_x, centers_y = [], []
for row in range(n_rows):
    for col in range(n_cols):
        centers_x.append(gminx + (col + 0.5) * cell_size)
        centers_y.append(gminy + (row + 0.5) * cell_size)
centers = np.column_stack([centers_x, centers_y])
predicted = model.predict(centers)
distance_map = round(float(np.median(nearest_distances(X, centers))))

half = cell_size / 2
cells = [
    Polygon([
        (cx - half, cy - half), (cx + half, cy - half),
        (cx + half, cy + half), (cx - half, cy + half),
        (cx - half, cy - half)
    ])
    for cx, cy in centers
]
grid_wgs84 = gpd.GeoDataFrame(
    {"predictedClass": predicted}, geometry=cells, crs=calc_epsg
).to_crs("EPSG:4326")
training_wgs84 = labeled[["class", "geometry"]]

{
    "trainingFeatures": training_wgs84.__geo_interface__,
    "gridFeatures": grid_wgs84.__geo_interface__,
    "calculationCrs": f"EPSG:{calc_epsg}",
    "classLabels": class_labels,
    "labeledCount": int(len(labeled)),
    "accuracyRandom": accuracy_random,
    "accuracyBlocks": accuracy_blocks,
    "classAccuracyRandom": class_accuracy_random,
    "classAccuracyBlocks": class_accuracy_blocks,
    "distanceRandom": distance_random,
    "distanceBlocks": distance_blocks,
    "distanceMap": distance_map,
    "gridCellCount": int(len(cells)),
    "crsWarning": crs_warning
}
```

## R

```{.webgeods-r #spatial-classification-r}
#| package: sf, randomForest, geojsonsf, jsonlite
library(sf)
library(geojsonsf)
library(randomForest)

# The same example survey the Python tab builds, from the same rule:
# 30 sites of 5 close-together points, three bands with undulating
# boundaries, one site in five on a local patch of the next class.
# Same arithmetic in the same order, so both languages produce
# identical points -- which is what makes the two tabs comparable at
# all.
fallback_points <- function() {
  site <- rep(0:29, each = 5)
  k <- rep(1:5, times = 30)
  dx <- c(0, 1, -0.6, -0.8, 0.5)[k]
  dy <- c(0, 0.4, 0.9, -0.7, -1)[k]
  cx <- (site %% 6 + 0.5) / 6 + ((site * 37) %% 11 - 5) / 110
  cy <- (site %/% 6 + 0.5) / 5 + ((site * 53) %% 13 - 6) / 130
  x <- cx + dx * 0.02
  y <- cy + dy * 0.02
  u <- x * 15
  v <- y * 10
  tri <- abs((2 * u) %% 8 - 4) - 2
  cls <- ifelse(v < 3 + tri, "south", ifelse(v < 6 + tri, "centre", "north"))
  next_class <- c(south = "centre", centre = "north", north = "south")
  patch <- site %% 5 == 2
  cls[patch] <- unname(next_class[cls[patch]])
  data.frame(lon = 12.4450 + x * 0.0150, lat = 41.8850 + y * 0.0120,
             class = cls, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}

data <- NULL
for (path in c("/uploaded.geojson", "/uploaded.shp", "/vsizip//uploaded.zip")) {
  data <- tryCatch(st_read(path, quiet = TRUE), error = function(e) NULL)
  if (!is.null(data)) break
}

crs_warning <- NULL
if (!is.null(data) && is.na(st_crs(data))) {
  st_crs(data) <- 4326
  crs_warning <- "No CRS found in the uploaded file — assuming WGS84 (EPSG:4326)."
} else if (!is.null(data) && !isTRUE(st_crs(data) == st_crs(4326))) {
  data <- st_transform(data, 4326)
}

if (is.null(data) || !("class" %in% names(data))) {
  data <- st_as_sf(fallback_points(), coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326)
  crs_warning <- NULL
}

labeled <- data[!is.na(data$class), ]
# The one step that decides classification vs. regression -- see
# section 5 below. Without this, randomForest() below would silently
# fit a REGRESSION on `class` instead.
labeled$class <- factor(as.character(labeled$class))

# UTM auto-pick from the bounding-box center -- see section 1 above.
bnd <- st_bbox(data)
center_lon <- (bnd[["xmin"]] + bnd[["xmax"]]) / 2
center_lat <- (bnd[["ymin"]] + bnd[["ymax"]]) / 2
utm_zone <- floor((center_lon + 180) / 6) + 1
calc_epsg <- if (center_lat >= 0) 32600 + utm_zone else 32700 + utm_zone

labeled_proj <- st_transform(labeled, calc_epsg)
coords_train <- st_coordinates(labeled_proj)

# A single UTM zone can map far-away points to infinity. Dropped
# here rather than failing outright: this article never compares
# points by position across languages, so partial exclusion doesn't
# desync anything.
finite_rows <- is.finite(coords_train[, 1]) & is.finite(coords_train[, 2])
if (!any(finite_rows)) {
  stop(paste0(
    "None of the labeled points could be projected into a single UTM zone ",
    "(EPSG:", calc_epsg, ") -- this dataset spans too wide an area for ",
    "this article's single-zone approach. Try a smaller, more local file."
  ))
}
coords_train <- coords_train[finite_rows, , drop = FALSE]
labeled_proj <- labeled_proj[finite_rows, ]

all_df <- data.frame(x = coords_train[, 1], y = coords_train[, 2], class = labeled_proj$class)

# Both the random folds below and the forest itself draw random
# numbers, so without a seed two runs of this cell give different
# answers. The Python tab passes random_state=0 for the same reason.
set.seed(0)

# 5-fold cross-validation two ways, as in the Python tab. Random folds:
# assigned within each class so every class keeps its share in every
# fold (base R has no stratified-fold function, but split() + sample()
# is the whole idea). Block folds: the same 4 x 4 grid and the same
# (bx + 2 * by) %% 5 rule as Python, no random numbers involved, so
# these folds are identical in both tabs.
n <- nrow(all_df)
random_folds <- integer(n)
for (idx in split(seq_len(n), all_df$class)) {
  random_folds[idx] <- sample(rep(0:4, length.out = length(idx)))
}

blocks_per_side <- 4
bmin_x <- min(all_df$x)
bmin_y <- min(all_df$y)
block_size <- max(max(all_df$x) - bmin_x, max(all_df$y) - bmin_y, 1e-6) / blocks_per_side
block_x <- pmin((all_df$x - bmin_x) %/% block_size, blocks_per_side - 1)
block_y <- pmin((all_df$y - bmin_y) %/% block_size, blocks_per_side - 1)
block_folds <- (block_x + 2 * block_y) %% 5

class_counts <- table(all_df$class)
can_validate <- length(class_counts) >= 2 && min(class_counts) >= 5 && n >= 10

cross_validated <- function(folds) {
  predicted <- character(n)
  for (f in unique(folds)) {
    test <- folds == f
    # droplevels(): randomForest() refuses a factor level with no rows,
    # which a block fold can leave behind by holding out every member
    # of a class that lives in one corner of the map.
    train_df <- droplevels(all_df[!test, ])
    fold_model <- randomForest(class ~ x + y, data = train_df, ntree = 100)
    predicted[test] <- as.character(predict(fold_model, newdata = all_df[test, ]))
  }
  truth <- as.character(all_df$class)
  # Overall and per class: one overall number can hide a model that is
  # perfect on the largest class and useless on another.
  by_class <- lapply(levels(all_df$class), function(cl) {
    jsonlite::unbox(round(mean(predicted[truth == cl] == cl), 3))
  })
  names(by_class) <- levels(all_df$class)
  list(accuracy = round(mean(predicted == truth), 3), by_class = by_class)
}

cv_random <- if (can_validate) cross_validated(random_folds) else NULL
cv_blocks <- if (can_validate) cross_validated(block_folds) else NULL

# How far each scheme's test points sit from the nearest point their
# forest trained on (median, in metres), as in the Python tab. A plain
# loop over every pair is fine at this size; a spatial index only pays
# off on far larger files.
nearest_distances <- function(train_xy, query_xy) {
  apply(query_xy, 1, function(p) sqrt(min((train_xy[, 1] - p[1])^2 + (train_xy[, 2] - p[2])^2)))
}
median_test_distance <- function(folds) {
  xy <- as.matrix(all_df[, c("x", "y")])
  median(unlist(lapply(unique(folds), function(f) {
    nearest_distances(xy[folds != f, , drop = FALSE], xy[folds == f, , drop = FALSE])
  })))
}
distance_random <- if (can_validate) round(median_test_distance(random_folds)) else NULL
distance_blocks <- if (can_validate) round(median_test_distance(block_folds)) else NULL

# Position is the ONLY predictor here (class ~ x + y): this
# demonstrates how a Random Forest turns labeled points into a
# surface, not a general land-cover classifier. Real covariates
# (spectral bands, elevation, soil type) would change what the model
# is actually learning. The map uses a forest trained on every point:
# the folds above were only for scoring it.
model <- randomForest(class ~ x + y, data = all_df, ntree = 100)

# The prediction surface: a regular grid covering the full extent, at
# the same fixed resolution the Python tab uses, so the two results
# are directly comparable. st_make_grid() builds it from an origin, a
# cell size and a cell count in one call.
coords_all <- st_coordinates(st_centroid(st_geometry(st_transform(data, calc_epsg))))
finite_all <- is.finite(coords_all[, 1]) & is.finite(coords_all[, 2])
gminx <- min(coords_all[finite_all, 1])
gmaxx <- max(coords_all[finite_all, 1])
gminy <- min(coords_all[finite_all, 2])
gmaxy <- max(coords_all[finite_all, 2])
cell_size <- max(gmaxx - gminx, gmaxy - gminy, 1e-6) / 10
n_cols <- max(1, ceiling((gmaxx - gminx) / cell_size))
n_rows <- max(1, ceiling((gmaxy - gminy) / cell_size))

grid <- st_make_grid(
  cellsize = cell_size,
  offset = c(gminx, gminy),
  n = c(n_cols, n_rows),
  crs = st_crs(calc_epsg)
)

# Each cell is classified by the point at its center: the model was
# trained on point coordinates, so that is the only thing it can be
# asked about.
grid_centers <- st_coordinates(st_centroid(grid))
predicted <- predict(model, newdata = data.frame(x = grid_centers[, 1], y = grid_centers[, 2]))
distance_map <- round(median(nearest_distances(as.matrix(all_df[, c("x", "y")]), grid_centers[, 1:2])))

grid_wgs84 <- st_transform(
  st_sf(predictedClass = as.character(predicted), geometry = grid),
  4326
)
training_wgs84 <- st_sf(
  class = as.character(labeled$class),
  geometry = st_geometry(labeled)
)

result <- list(
  calculationCrs = jsonlite::unbox(paste0("EPSG:", calc_epsg)),
  classLabels = sort(levels(labeled_proj$class)),
  labeledCount = jsonlite::unbox(as.integer(nrow(labeled))),
  accuracyRandom = if (is.null(cv_random)) NULL else jsonlite::unbox(cv_random$accuracy),
  accuracyBlocks = if (is.null(cv_blocks)) NULL else jsonlite::unbox(cv_blocks$accuracy),
  classAccuracyRandom = if (is.null(cv_random)) NULL else cv_random$by_class,
  classAccuracyBlocks = if (is.null(cv_blocks)) NULL else cv_blocks$by_class,
  distanceRandom = if (is.null(distance_random)) NULL else jsonlite::unbox(distance_random),
  distanceBlocks = if (is.null(distance_blocks)) NULL else jsonlite::unbox(distance_blocks),
  distanceMap = jsonlite::unbox(distance_map),
  gridCellCount = jsonlite::unbox(as.integer(length(grid))),
  modelType = jsonlite::unbox(model$type),
  crsWarning = if (is.null(crs_warning)) NULL else jsonlite::unbox(crs_warning)
)
out <- jsonlite::fromJSON(jsonlite::toJSON(result, null = "null"), simplifyVector = FALSE)

# The two GeoJSON payloads are attached AFTER that round-trip, not
# inside it: sf_geojson() already returns finished JSON, and passing
# it through toJSON() a second time would turn every scalar inside it
# ("type": "Feature") back into a one-element array.
out$gridFeatures <- jsonlite::fromJSON(sf_geojson(grid_wgs84), simplifyVector = FALSE)
out$trainingFeatures <- jsonlite::fromJSON(sf_geojson(training_wgs84), simplifyVector = FALSE)
out
```

The filled grid is the predicted surface; the dots on top are the
labeled training points, colored the same way. Each language draws
onto its own map sources, so running either one on its own is enough
to see a result.

Run both and the two surfaces won't match everywhere. They cover
exactly the same ground and start from identical points (the two cells
build the survey from the same arithmetic rule), but they don't label
every cell the same way. It's tempting to read that as Python
disagreeing with R. It isn't: both cells fix a seed so their output is
reproducible, and changing that number moves the surface just as much
as switching language does. A forest retrained disagrees with itself
about as much as the two languages disagree with each other.

## 4. How good is that surface?

Both cells score the model with 5-fold cross-validation: the points
are split into five groups, each group is held out in turn while a
forest trains on the other four, and in the end every point has been
predicted once by a model that never saw it. The only difference
between the two rows of each stat card is *how* the points are split
into groups.

**Random folds** scatter the held-out points across the whole map.
On the built-in survey that scores about **0.76–0.81**, in either
language, against 0.33 for guessing among three classes. It looks
like a usable map.

**Spatial blocks** cut the area into a 4 × 4 grid and hold out whole
blocks at a time. Same points, same forest, same number of trees:
about **0.54–0.59**. Twenty points lower, in every one of the five
seeds tried per language.

Nothing about the model changed between the two rows, only the
question being asked. A random fold almost never holds out a whole
site: four of a test point's five site-mates, a few metres away, are
still in training, and the forest can simply copy them. Even a point
on one of the patches comes out right, because its site-mates on the
same patch were seen. Hold out a whole block and the patch goes out
with it: now the model has to predict it from the sites around it,
which say something else.

So which number describes the map? Neither exactly, and the stat
cards' last row says why. A cross-validated score only holds for
predictions made about as far from the data as its test points were.
Random test points sit a median **27 m** from the nearest training
point: a site-mate. Block test points sit about **193 m** away. The
map's own grid cells, the places it is actually asked about, sit
about **73 m** from the nearest sample, in between. The random score
answers an easier question than the map faces, the blocks score a
harder one.

In a separate run (in Python, on the same points, not on this page),
the block grids whose test distances came closest to the map's,
10 × 10 and 12 × 12 (blocks about 100–120 m across instead of 300),
scored **0.61–0.65**. That's roughly the honest figure for this map:
the random score overstates it by 10 to 20 points, the 4 × 4 blocks
understate it by up to about 10. Other grid sizes in the same run
landed anywhere from 0.52 to 0.72, so a fixed grid is a crude way to
match distances; dedicated methods for spatial validation
(nearest-neighbour distance matching, NNDM and its variants) do it
with more care. The 4 × 4 blocks are the safer number to quote, not
the exact one.

The per-class numbers show where the gap comes from. Under random
folds `centre`, the narrow middle band squeezed between the other two,
looks nearly as well learned as the rest, around 0.7. Under blocks it
drops to about **0.35**, barely above chance: with its own
neighbourhood removed, the forest can't tell the thin middle band
from the wide ones on either side. One overall number, from either
scheme, would have hidden that the model has essentially learned two
of the three classes.

Both numbers move from run to run, too. The block folds are fixed
(the same arithmetic rule in both tabs, so they're identical), but the
forest itself draws random numbers, and the random folds are drawn by
each language's own generator, so Python and R hold out *different*
points there. The ranges above overlap between languages, and five
seeds each are nowhere near enough to rank scikit-learn against
randomForest. What doesn't move is the gap: random folds beat blocks
by a wide margin every time, in both.

One more thing the folds don't do: change the map. Every forest
trained inside the cross-validation is thrown away once it has been
scored. The map comes from a separate forest trained on all 150
points, the usual practice, since cross-validation scores the *way*
the model is fitted rather than one particular fitted forest. The
choice of scheme would start changing the map only if it were used to
choose something, a smoothing setting say, and random folds would
then reward the forest that copies its neighbours most faithfully.

## 5. A silent switch: classification vs. regression

The disagreements above are a model being unsure. This one is
different: a model quietly solving a different problem.

scikit-learn's `RandomForestClassifier` and R's general-purpose
`randomForest()` decide what to do very differently. scikit-learn is
unambiguous: you asked for a *Classifier*, so it classifies,
whatever the labels look like. R's `randomForest()` instead looks at
the *type* of the target column, and the two ways of getting this
wrong fail very differently:

- A plain **character** column (`"north"`/`"south"`, never wrapped in
  `factor()`) fails loudly. R can't compute a regression mean on
  text, so the fit errors out immediately with something like
  `non-numeric argument to binary operator`. Annoying, but safe: you
  find out right away.
- A column of **numbers standing in for classes** (`0`/`1`, or a
  status code read straight out of a file) is the dangerous one: it
  fits without complaint and silently runs a **regression** instead of
  a classification. No error, no warning, just a different kind of
  model whose predictions no longer look like class labels at all.

The R cell above already does this correctly (`factor(as.character(...))`
before the fit): `modelType` in its stat card reads `classification`.
Here's the realistic failure case: the exact same points, with `class`
read in as `0`/`1`/`2` instead of `"south"`/`"centre"`/`"north"` (exactly what
happens if a class column arrives as a numeric status code), and that
one `factor()` step skipped, run live:

```{.webgeods-r #spatial-classification-r-nofactor}
#| package: sf, randomForest, jsonlite
library(randomForest)

# The same survey as the cell above, built from the same rule.
site <- rep(0:29, each = 5)
k <- rep(1:5, times = 30)
x <- (site %% 6 + 0.5) / 6 + ((site * 37) %% 11 - 5) / 110 + c(0, 1, -0.6, -0.8, 0.5)[k] * 0.02
y <- (site %/% 6 + 0.5) / 5 + ((site * 53) %% 13 - 6) / 130 + c(0, 0.4, 0.9, -0.7, -1)[k] * 0.02
tri <- abs((2 * (x * 15)) %% 8 - 4) - 2
cls <- ifelse(y * 10 < 3 + tri, "south", ifelse(y * 10 < 6 + tri, "centre", "north"))
next_class <- c(south = "centre", centre = "north", north = "south")
patch <- site %% 5 == 2
cls[patch] <- unname(next_class[cls[patch]])
lon <- 12.4450 + x * 0.0150
lat <- 41.8850 + y * 0.0120

# The one difference: `class` arrives as a NUMERIC status code
# (0 = south, 1 = centre, 2 = north) and is NOT wrapped in factor(),
# unlike the cell above. A character column here would error
# immediately (see the prose above); a numeric one fits silently.
class_code <- c(south = 0, centre = 1, north = 2)[cls]

train_df <- data.frame(x = lon, y = lat, class = unname(class_code))
model <- randomForest(class ~ x + y, data = train_df, ntree = 100)

result <- list(
  modelType = jsonlite::unbox(model$type),
  sampleTrueClass = jsonlite::unbox(train_df$class[1]),
  samplePrediction = jsonlite::unbox(as.numeric(predict(model, train_df[1, ])))
)
jsonlite::fromJSON(jsonlite::toJSON(result, null = "null"), simplifyVector = FALSE)
```

::: {#lab-nofactor}
:::

`model$type` reads `regression`, and `predict()` on a point whose true
class was `0` (`south`) returns something like `0.044`, not the class
`0` itself: a *regression estimate*, an average of the training
codes, that happens to land near it. On a point near a boundary it
would land somewhere in between, a `0.7` that is no class at all. Nothing in the output says a switch happened; the only way to
notice is checking `model$type` yourself, which is exactly what
production code should do.

::: {.callout-note}
This is real, verified behavior of `randomForest()`, run live on this
page, not an edge case invented for the article: the R cell in
section 3 above does the correct `factor()` coercion, one line
different from the cell above. scikit-learn's separate `Classifier`/
`Regressor` classes make the same mistake structurally impossible: the
class you instantiate *is* the decision, made once, up front.
:::
